title: Opportunities for Odor: Experiences with Smell and Implications for Technology
research_question: To investigate the subjective experience of smell and the emotions that accompany it, and to explore the implications of these experiences for smell-enhanced technology design.

participants.description: 439 participants (52.8% female) living in the US (95% grown up in US), aged 18 to 67 years (M = 31.5, SD = 10.0). A majority (84%) indicated being sensitive to smell.
participants.recruitment: Administered through a crowdsourcing platform (Amazon Mechanical Turk)

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Participants' own personally memorable smell experiences (narratives).
Six inspirational examples of existing smell technologies (e.g., Olfoto, Smelling Screen, Digital Smell, Scent Dress, Mobile Smell App, Smell-enhanced cinema) to prompt envisioning.

measures.instrument: Likert scale ('not personally relevant at all' to 'very personally relevant')
Open and closed questions (social context, place, location, time)
List of 72 adjectives (Geneva Emotion and Odor Scale - GEOS) and open feedback

measures.construct: Perceived pleasantness, intensity, and familiarity of smell

measures.instrument: List of 101 affective terms (Scherer) and free-text field
Open-ended questions on enhancing experience, desired technology, desirability rationale, other ideas

findings.antecedent: Smell experience (Category 1: Associating the past with a smell)
findings.consequent: Positive emotional experience (e.g., courageousness, excitement)
findings.mechanism: Strong association of smell with particular past moments, evoking specific emotions.
findings.quote: Although this category is dominated by positive experiences (n = 127), negative experiences were also reported (n = 27)

findings.antecedent: Smell experience (Category 2: Remembering through a smell)
findings.consequent: Reminders of childhood and past events, evoking feelings of being taken back in time
findings.mechanism: Indirect link from present experienced smell stimulus to past events, people, or places.
findings.quote: Most stories in this category contain reminders of childhood described as 'sweet', 'reassuring' and 'nostalgic'

findings.antecedent: Smell experience (Category 3: Smell perceived as stimulating)
findings.consequent: Positive emotional experience (e.g., delighted, enthusiastic, joyous, serene)
findings.mechanism: Smells perceived as fresh, pure, groovy, pleasant, stimulating, refreshing.
findings.quote: The stories in this category described experiences with a unique, mostly unknown smell (all stories, except one, were positive).

findings.antecedent: Smell experience (Category 7: Smell invading private and public spaces)
findings.consequent: Negative emotional experience (e.g., annoyed, anxious, disgusted, uncomfortable) and behavioral response (e.g., leaving the house)
findings.mechanism: Loss of control over a lingering, foul, nauseous, penetrating, and persistent smell.
findings.quote: The loss of control over the smell was linked to the lingering quality of the smell... this category mainly contains negative experiences

findings.antecedent: Smell experience (Category 8: Social interaction is affected by the smell)
findings.consequent: Negative social interaction (e.g., bitter, distressed, insulted emotions, impeded communication)
findings.mechanism: A person's own smell or the smell of others (nauseous, penetrating, sickening) negatively affecting interaction.
findings.quote: Smell negatively affected the interaction among people and their togetherness... This set of stories (overall negative experiences, apart from two)

findings.antecedent: Smell experience (Category 9: Smell changes mood, attitude and behavior)
findings.consequent: Change in mood, attitude, or behavior (e.g., feeling hopeful, less lonely)
findings.mechanism: Smells (e.g., fresh, reassuring, spring-like) actively regulate mood and can be used to change one's emotional state.
findings.quote: This category contains 23 stories, which underlined the power of smells to change a person's mood, attitude, or behavior.

findings.antecedent: Smell experience (Category 10: Smell builds up and changes expectations)
findings.consequent: Anticipation and surprise (e.g., mouthwatering, pleasantly surprising)
findings.mechanism: Smell can build up expectations until contact with the trigger, or exceed expectations leading to surprise.
findings.quote: This category shows the potential of smell to build up expectations and to surprise.

findings.consequent: Story length
findings.mechanism: Negative stories tended to be slightly longer than positive stories, though not statistically significant.
findings.quote: On average, negative stories tended to be slightly longer (M = 90 words) than positive stories (M = 79 words), but the difference is statistically not significant (U = 14600, p = .063, r = .09).

findings.consequent: Reported smell qualities
findings.mechanism: Positive stories frequently described smells as pleasant (60%), fresh (42%), sweet (38%), clean (31%), and mouthwatering (30%).
findings.quote: The most frequent smell qualities reported in positive stories were pleasant (60%), fresh (42%), sweet (38%), clean (31%), and mouthwatering (30%).

findings.consequent: Reported smell qualities
findings.mechanism: Negative stories frequently described smells as unpleasant (62%), penetrating (55%), heavy (54%), foul (53%), and nauseous (51%).
findings.quote: Smells in negative stories were described as unpleasant (62%), penetrating (55%), heavy (54%), foul (53%), and nauseous (51%).

findings.consequent: Reported smell qualities
findings.mechanism: Ambivalent stories frequently described smells as fresh (39%), pleasant (32%), mouth-watering (32%), attractive (26%), and penetrating (23%).
findings.quote: In ambivalent stories the smell was perceived as fresh (39%), pleasant (32%), mouth-watering (32%), attractive (26%), and penetrating (23%).

findings.consequent: Experienced emotions
findings.mechanism: Positive experiences frequently described emotions as happy (63%), pleased (53%), joyous (42%), delighted (41%), and excited (39%).
findings.quote: participants' used the affective terms happy (63%), pleased (53%), joyous (42%), delighted (41%), and excited (39%) in positive stories

findings.consequent: Experienced emotions
findings.mechanism: Negative experiences frequently described emotions as uncomfortable (55%), disgusted (51%), distressed (43%), miserable (42%), and taken aback (29%).
findings.quote: uncomfortable (55%), disgusted (51%), distressed (43%), miserable (42%), and taken aback (29%) in negative stories.

findings.consequent: Experienced emotions
findings.mechanism: Ambivalent experiences most frequently described as happy (42%), excited (39%), enthusiastic (35%), joyous (32%), and serene (29%).
findings.quote: Ambivalent experiences were most frequently described as happy (42%), excited (39%), enthusiastic (35%), joyous (32%), and serene (29%).

findings.antecedent: Smell-enhanced technology (e.g., mobile phone, photo or video camera)
findings.consequent: Ability to capture and share personal memorable smell experiences
findings.mechanism: Participants desired to capture pleasant smells (e.g., from childhood) and release them in the present, suggesting real-time smell-enhanced technologies.
findings.quote: The desire for capturing and sharing these experiences enhanced with smell becomes prevalent and suggests design implications for real-time smell-enhanced technologies

findings.consequent: Support for quick decision-making (e.g., online shopping, dating)
findings.mechanism: Smells are seen as powerful for supporting quick, implicit judgments.
findings.quote: smells are seen as very powerful for supporting quick decision-making (e.g., smell-enhanced website navigation and searching).

findings.consequent: Regulation of mood (e.g., relive good experiences, calm down)
findings.mechanism: Smell can have a regulating impact on a person's mood and can be used to regulate mood.
findings.quote: The third idea shows a direct link to Category 9 and the potential of smell to change mood.

findings.consequent: Avoidance of embarrassing moments in social interactions
findings.mechanism: Technology could provide invisible cues about body smell levels to prevent discomfort or insult.
findings.quote: Finally, the sixth idea is linked to Category 8, aiming to avoid embarrassing moments in social interactions.

findings.antecedent: Always available access to memory-based smell technology
findings.consequent: Uniqueness of smell experience
findings.mechanism: The power of smell might not persist if always available, leading to habituation and making the experience 'common place'.
findings.quote: The power of smell might not persist if always available, thus participants suggested to either restrict the access and retrieval of smells to special times

findings.consequent: Reminder effectiveness for important events
findings.mechanism: Smell can provide a pleasant or powerful (bad smell) reminder that is not easily ignored, unlike visual/auditory reminders.
findings.quote: A smell can provide a pleasant reminder to say ‘it is time to call your mom’... if more critical, bad smells can be very powerful as a reminder and are not easily ignored

findings.antecedent: Smell-enhanced technology (e.g., digitized incense stick, photo album)
findings.consequent: Storytelling and memory recall about loved ones
findings.mechanism: Smells can serve as anchor points for keeping memories alive and triggering new stories about past events and people.
findings.quote: A technology that stimulates storytelling around a digitized version of an incense stick... using the smells as anchor points for keeping the memory alive

mechanisms: Associative learning principles for hedonic response to smells.
Direct and intense contact of smell with neural substrates of emotion and memory.
Smell's power to induce mood changes and regulate emotional states.
Smell's ability to build up expectations and create surprise.
Smell's capacity to act as a powerful, less ignorable reminder compared to other modalities.
moderators: Cultural and geographical differences (mentioned as a limitation for generalizability).
implementation_implications: Design technologies for capturing and sharing personal memorable smells (e.g., via social media, mobile devices) for memory recall and social bonding.
Develop smell-enhanced tools to support quick decision-making in online contexts (e.g., shopping, dating).
Create smell technologies for active and passive mood regulation and wellbeing support (e.g., stress reduction, mood enhancement).
Integrate smell with existing technologies and everyday objects (e.g., music, ads, jewelry) to enrich experiences.
Design systems for body smell awareness to avoid social embarrassment and improve comfort.
Consider the potential for misuse, manipulation, health risks, and copyright issues in smell technology design.
Design for 'first time' and 'momentary' smell experiences to leverage their impact and avoid habituation.
Explore designing with 'bad smells' for specific purposes like critical reminders, using intensity manipulation.
limitations: Reliance on Amazon Mechanical Turk for recruitment limits generalizability to the US population and may not represent more diverse experiences with smell.
Online questionnaire format may influence how people narrate experiences and limits in-depth dialogue compared to interviews.
The study provides an overview of emerging smell-enhanced technologies, suggesting a need for more in-depth research into specific categories.
